sources.title: ACME E-FIELD Flames — Advanced Combustion via Microgravity Experiments Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames — approach
sources.text: The gas-jet burner is used to create a small, focused flame for detailed ion-driven convection studies while the coflow burner surrounds the fuel jet with a weak synthetic air flow to enable flame stability and soot behavior analysis. A high-voltage copper mesh electrode positioned above the burner tip generated an electric field with controlled polarity and strength. The electric field interacts with ions generated through chemi-ionization during combustion, driving ion-driving convection and influencing flame behavior. Methane and ethylene were used as fuels and diluted with nitrogen to control flame strength. Dilution levels were varied to explore a range of combustion dynamics, from highly stable to near-extinction flames.

sources.title: Quantitative Studies of Cool Flame Transitions at Radiation / Stretch Extinction Using Counterflow Flames — hypothesis
sources.text: This investigation attempts to answer the critical question as to what conditions causes the hot flames transfer to cool flames and how the cool flame flammable region is related to hot flame flammability limit and extinction limit. The investigation hypothesizes that factors such as oxygen concentration, dilution, pressure, diffusion, and convection transport processes affect the cool flame transition.

sources.title: SLICE — Structure and Liftoff In Combustion Experiment — approach
sources.text: The SLICE apparatus consisted of a fan-driven flow duct, exchangeable burner tubes, and integrated sensors to measure flow rates and temperature. This setup used several fuels such as methane, ethylene, and nitrogen-diluted mixtures. Flames were then manually ignited and observed under controlled coflow air conditions. A high resolution camera captured still images while sensor data was overlaid on these images. Calibration tests for airflow velocity, soot measurement, and the fans were conducted to ensure the accuracy of the results. More than 4,000 high-resolution images were captured across 13 testing experiments. Data was then analyzed to correlate flame structure with stability with flow dynamics and fuel properties.

sources.title: BASS-II maps solid-fuel burning down to 13.6 % O2
sources.text: BASS-II ran 129 tests with initial O2 between 13.6 and 22.2 % vol, mostly on PMMA, SIBAL (cotton-fiberglass fabric), Nomex. Flow annotations record extinction in 15 tests, blow-off in 3 and no ignition in 1. Limitation: Outcome annotations are free text; flow units to be confirmed in the BASS-II documentation; flame-spread rates are in the raw video data.

sources.title: Cool flames: combustion at 500–1000 K
sources.text: Cool diffusion flames have peak temperatures of about 500–1000 K. FLEX, CFI and CFI-G studied them on droplets and burners in microgravity. Limitation: Research fuels and configurations; relevance to cabin fires is an open question, not a finding.

sources.title: More oxygen: droplet flames more often survive to burnout
sources.text: FLEX droplet tests in N2-only atmospheres that ended in flame extinction before burnout — Heptane: 5/17 at 21 % O2 vs 0/11 at 30–34 % O2; Methanol: 9/12 at 21 % O2 vs 2/13 at 30–34 % O2. Remaining tests ended in burnout ('completion') or droplet disruption. Limitation: Isolated droplets, two fuels; 'extinction' here means the flame went out before the droplet was consumed (often radiative), not the action of an extinguisher. Counts, not a model.

sources.title: No partial-gravity combustion data yet
sources.text: PSI currently holds no combustion data at lunar or martian gravity. The challenge notes that microgravity and normal-gravity results can bound intermediate gravity levels, and that E-FIELD (PSI-22) mimicked partial gravity with ion-driven forces. Limitation: Bounding is not interpolation: behaviour at 1/6 g may not lie between the two cases for every metric.

top_passage.text: Current NASA spacecraft materials selection is based on a standard test method (NASA–STD–6001 Test 1) that segregates material based on 1-g behavior without consideration of low gravity effects. A critical element of this understanding is the radiative heat emission from the flame. These results are used in first order models and predictions of heat release in spacecraft fires and as a means to extend heat release data from tests like the NASA cone calorimeter test (NASA–STD–6001 Test 2) to a performance-based material selection process. Using nitrogen as a flame suppressant in microgravity provides a direct link to current and planned extinguishment techniques.

top_passage.text: Conventional gaseous fuels including hydrogen, methane, and ethylene will be used. Hydrogen is the simplest fuel and its reaction mechanism is also reasonably established. Methane is the simplest hydrocarbon and extensive studies have been conducted on its combustion chemistry. Ethylene is a typical sooty fuel and is also an important intermediate for the oxidation of higher hydrocarbons. Diluents mixed with fuel are to include nitrogen and helium to adjust mixture diffusivities, and carbon dioxide to influence flame radiation characteristics.
